subject: Environment
sub_topic: Wetland conservation — Ramsar sites in India

concepts.name: Ramsar Convention: Foundation, Structure, and Legal Nature
key_dimensions: Year of adoption (1971), entry into force (1975), and India's accession year (1982) — common date-confusion trap
Non-binding vs. binding nature of Ramsar obligations and the 'wise use' principle as its cornerstone
Three pillars: wise use of all wetlands, designation of Ramsar sites, international cooperation
Secretariat location (Gland, Switzerland) and its relationship with IUCN — frequently confused

concepts.name: Definition of 'Wetlands' under Ramsar vs. Indian Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules
key_dimensions: Ramsar's broad definition: marshes, fens, peatlands, water — natural or artificial, permanent or temporary, static or flowing, fresh/brackish/salt
India's Wetlands Rules 2017 definition and what it explicitly EXCLUDES (paddy fields, water bodies <2.25 ha) — classic exclusion trap
Difference between Ramsar's inclusion of marine waters up to 6m depth at low tide vs. India's regulatory scope
Why rivers per se are not classified as wetlands under Indian rules — overlap with River Regulation Zone

concepts.name: Criteria for Ramsar Site Designation (9 Criteria across 3 Groups)
key_dimensions: Group A (Criteria 1–2): Representative/rare/unique wetlands and threatened species/ecological communities
Group B — Biodiversity criteria: Criteria 3–9 covering waterbirds, fish, indigenous fish, important food source, etc.
A site needs to meet ONLY ONE criterion to qualify — the 'only one' trap
India-specific: which criteria most Indian Ramsar sites are designated under (waterbird criterion vs. biodiversity criterion)

concepts.name: Montreux Record: Purpose, Mechanism, and Indian Sites
key_dimensions: Definition: Register of Ramsar sites where changes in ecological character have occurred, are occurring, or are likely to occur
Mechanism: Countries can self-nominate or the Standing Committee can recommend; removal requires demonstrated restoration
Indian sites on Montreux Record: Keoladeo (Ghana) National Park and Loktak Lake — both added and one removed (Keoladeo removed in 2011)
UPSC trap: Chilika Lake was on Montreux Record and successfully REMOVED (2002) — model restoration case; Loktak remains listed

concepts.name: Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2017: Key Provisions and Regulatory Architecture
key_dimensions: Replaces Wetland Rules 2010 — key differences: removal of 'prohibited activities' list replaced by 'wise use' approach
State Wetland Authority (SWA) as the primary regulatory body — composition and powers
National Wetland Authority: Why India does NOT have a statutory National Wetland Authority (advisory role only) — institutional gap trap
Activities requiring prior permission vs. outright prohibited activities under 2017 Rules — frequently tested boundary

concepts.name: India's Ramsar Sites: Numbers, Distribution, and Recent Additions
key_dimensions: India has the highest number of Ramsar sites in South Asia — current count trajectory (42 as of 2023, subject to updates)
States with most Ramsar sites: Tamil Nadu leads — a counter-intuitive fact UPSC exploits
Sites added in one go (2022 batch of 11 sites was a landmark) — pattern of additions around CoP years
Only site in a Union Territory: Sultanpur (Haryana) vs. sites in island UTs — geographic spread trap

concepts.name: Iconic Indian Ramsar Sites: Ecological Significance and Uniqueness
key_dimensions: Chilika Lake: Largest coastal lagoon in Asia, not largest wetland — precision trap; habitat for Irrawaddy dolphins
Sundarbans: Ramsar site AND UNESCO World Heritage Site AND Tiger Reserve — triple-designation overlap
Loktak Lake: Only floating national park (Keibul Lamjao) within a Ramsar site; phumdis are unique floating biomass
Wular Lake: Largest freshwater lake in India — located in J&K, strategic and ecological significance

concepts.name: Ramsar Sites and Overlap with Other Designations (PA Network, Biosphere Reserves, World Heritage)
key_dimensions: Ramsar sites vs. Protected Areas under Wildlife Protection Act — Ramsar designation does NOT automatically confer PA status
Sites that are simultaneously Biosphere Reserves: e.g., Sundarbans, Gulf of Mannar — implications for management authority
UNESCO World Heritage Sites that are also Ramsar sites in India — Keoladeo is both; management conflicts
UPSC trap: A Ramsar site can include privately owned land and agricultural land — common misconception

concepts.name: Ecological Functions and Ecosystem Services of Wetlands
key_dimensions: Provisioning services: fisheries, water supply, genetic resources
Regulating services: flood control, groundwater recharge, carbon sequestration — wetlands as 'blue carbon' stores
Cultural services: tourism, sacred groves associated with wetlands, traditional knowledge systems
UPSC angle: Wetlands store ~30% of terrestrial carbon (peatlands) despite covering only ~6% of land surface — disproportionate climate role

concepts.name: Threats to Wetlands: Classification and India-Specific Drivers
key_dimensions: Direct threats: encroachment, conversion to agriculture (paddy paradox — paddy fields not protected but drain natural wetlands)
Pollution threats: agricultural run-off (eutrophication), industrial effluents, plastic — Bellandur Lake case study
Hydrological threats: upstream damming reducing inflow (Loktak case with Ithai Barrage), groundwater extraction
Climate change threats: sea-level rise affecting coastal Ramsar sites, altered precipitation patterns — long-term irreversibility angle

concepts.name: National Wetland Conservation Programme (NWCP) and Amrit Dharohar Scheme
key_dimensions: NWCP launched by MoEFCC — funding pattern (centrally sponsored, now merged into broader schemes), identification of 115 wetlands
Amrit Dharohar Scheme (2023 Budget): Focus on 75 Ramsar sites, community involvement, eco-tourism, carbon stock — Budget announcement vs. implementation
Difference between NWCP-identified wetlands and Ramsar-designated wetlands — not all 115 NWCP wetlands are Ramsar sites
Wetland Mitras: Community stewardship model under Amrit Dharohar — roles and limitations

concepts.name: Wise Use Principle: Ramsar's Core Concept and Its Application
key_dimensions: Definition: 'Maintenance of ecological character achieved through implementation of ecosystem approaches within sustainable development context'
Not equivalent to 'no use' — allows sustainable utilization; distinction from strict preservation
Ramsar Handbooks on Wise Use — non-binding guidance tools vs. Convention obligations
India's challenge: Reconciling wise use with urban wetland encroachment and 'deemed forest' equivalent status demands

concepts.name: Ecological Character and Its Change: Ramsar's Core Monitoring Obligation
key_dimensions: Ecological character = combination of ecosystem components, processes, and services that characterize the wetland at a given point in time
Contracting Parties must notify Ramsar Secretariat of adverse change (Article 3.2) — reporting obligation often missed by India
Difference between 'change in ecological character' triggering Montreux Record vs. routine degradation
UPSC trap: India's compliance gap — several sites showing degradation not reported under Article 3.2

concepts.name: Ramsar's Conference of Parties (CoP): Structure, Frequency, and Key Resolutions Affecting India
key_dimensions: CoP meets every 3 years — Standing Committee governs between CoPs; Scientific and Technical Review Panel (STRP) advises
CoP13 (Dubai, 2018) and CoP14 (Wuhan-Geneva, 2022) — resolutions on urban wetlands, wetland city accreditation
Wetland City Accreditation under Ramsar: No Indian city accredited yet (as of 2023) — gap vs. China's multiple accredited cities
Resolution on 'other effective area-based conservation measures' (OECMs) and wetlands — overlap with CBD 30x30 target

concepts.name: Mangroves as a Special Wetland Category: Governance and Conservation
key_dimensions: Mangroves classified as wetlands under Ramsar but also regulated under CRZ (Coastal Regulation Zone) Notification — dual governance trap
CRZ 2019: Mangroves given highest protection regardless of notified area — 'no-development zone' of 50m vs. earlier provisions
India's mangrove cover trends (slight increase recently per FSI reports) vs. quality degradation
UPSC trap: Sundarbans mangroves are in both India AND Bangladesh — transboundary Ramsar site concept; India's portion is a Ramsar site while Bangladesh's Sundarbans is a separate Ramsar site

concepts.name: High Altitude Wetlands as Ramsar Sites: Special Characteristics
key_dimensions: Tso Kar Wetland Complex (Ladakh): India's 42nd Ramsar site; cold desert, high altitude — added 2020
Tsomoriri: High altitude lake in Ladakh — habitat for Black-necked Crane (Schedule I species); both Ramsar and Biosphere Reserve
Ecological functions unique to high-altitude wetlands: glacial melt dependency, vulnerability to climate change and permafrost thaw
Geopolitical sensitivity: High-altitude Ramsar sites in Ladakh — border area restrictions on research and access

concepts.name: Urban Wetlands: Regulatory Challenges and Case Studies
key_dimensions: Urban wetlands not covered under CRZ or Forest Conservation Act — governance vacuum exploited for real estate development
Supreme Court interventions: Pallikaranai marshland (Chennai), Aarey Colony (Mumbai) — judicial vs. regulatory protection
Delhi's wetlands: Hauz Khas, Bhalswa — deterioration despite National Green Tribunal orders; NGT's limited enforcement capacity
Ramsar's Urban Wetland Initiative and why no Indian urban wetland has received formal protection under a comprehensive urban wetland policy

concepts.name: Wetlands and Indigenous/Local Communities: Rights vs. Conservation
key_dimensions: Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers Act (FRA) 2006 — community forest rights over wetlands within forest areas
Loktak Lake: Meitei community's traditional relationship vs. conservation restrictions — conflict model
Chilika Lake: Fisher communities vs. aquaculture intrusion — Supreme Court order on prawn gheries (1996 case)
Ramsar's recognition of indigenous rights vs. India's practice of displacement for wetland conservation — implementation gap

concepts.name: Wetland-Biodiversity Nexus: Keystone Species and Migration Routes
key_dimensions: Central Asian Flyway (CAF): India's wetlands as critical stopover — 29 countries, covers migratory birds; India is signatory to CAF Action Plan (2018)
Critically endangered species dependent on Ramsar sites: Siberian Crane (Keoladeo), Gangetic River Dolphin (Ganga wetlands), Fishing Cat
Flamingo ecology: Rann of Kutch (not a Ramsar site) vs. Sambhar Lake (Ramsar site) — breeding vs. foraging habitat distinction
UPSC trap: Not all Important Bird Areas (IBAs) identified by Birdlife International are Ramsar sites — different criteria and different designating bodies

concepts.name: Carbon Sequestration Role of Wetlands: Blue Carbon and Climate Policy Linkages
key_dimensions: Peatlands store twice the carbon of world's forests despite covering 3% of land — magnitude trap in MCQs
Blue carbon ecosystems: mangroves, seagrasses, salt marshes — Ramsar's role in promoting blue carbon accounting
India's NDC and wetland conservation: Wetland restoration as a nature-based solution (NbS) for climate mitigation
UNFCCC vs. Ramsar mandate overlap: Wetland drainage is a source of GHG emissions; drainage of peatlands accounts for ~5% of global CO2 emissions
